opus-5.5.text:
I think computer use is one of the most natural extensions of what these models can already do. If you want an agent that's actually useful in someone's day-to-day life, it has to operate in the same environment people do, and for most knowledge work that's a screen, a browser, a bunch of apps that were never designed with an API in mind. Computer use is the bridge. It lets the model meet the world where it is, instead of waiting for every service to expose a clean tool interface.

What's interesting to me is that it changes the shape of the interaction. With chat, you're in a tight loop: you ask, it answers, you read it. With computer use, you delegate. You say "go book this," "fill out these forms," "pull this data from five different dashboards," and the model is taking dozens of actions on its own. That means the hard problems shift. It's less about whether the model knows the answer and more about whether it can plan over a long horizon, recover when a page doesn't load the way it expected, and know when to stop and check in with you instead of barreling ahead.

So for me, a lot of the most important research questions are about trust and collaboration. How does the agent communicate what it's doing? How do you, as a person, stay in the loop without micromanaging? When should it ask for confirmation, especially for things that are irreversible, like sending an email or making a purchase? Getting that right is as much a product and design problem as a modeling problem.

I'd also say it's early. The models are still slow, they make silly mistakes clicking around, and the evals are hard to build because real environments are messy. But I think it's a really important capability to invest in, because it's a step toward models that aren't just answering questions but are actually doing work alongside you. Eventually I think it blends together: the agent uses an API when there is one, a browser when there isn't, writes code when that's easier, and you don't really care which. Computer use is the piece that makes that general.

r001.rationale: It explicitly describes computer use as enabling delegation, with examples such as booking, filling forms, and gathering data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of computer use as the thing that closes the gap between a model that can reason about a task and a model that can actually finish it. For a long time, agents were limited to whatever had an API. If a tool exposed clean endpoints, the model could use it. If it didn't, you were stuck. But most of the real work people do lives inside interfaces that were built for humans: browsers, spreadsheets, internal dashboards, legacy enterprise software that nobody is ever going to write an integration for. Computer use means the model can operate in that world the way a person would, by looking at the screen, moving the cursor, typing, clicking, scrolling.

So in that sense it's less a feature and more a general-purpose actuator. Reasoning, tool use, memory, planning, all of that was already developing, but without a way to touch the environment broadly, agents hit a ceiling pretty quickly. Computer use removes the ceiling. It lets you take a long, messy, multi-step task, like filling out a form across three systems or reconciling data between two tools, and hand the whole thing off.

What I find most interesting is how it changes what you have to get right in the model. It's not just about perception, recognizing what's on the screen. It's about being careful. You have to notice when something unexpected happens, when a dialog pops up, when an action didn't do what you thought, and recover gracefully. You have to know when to stop and ask instead of plowing forward. Those are honestly the same qualities you'd want in a good junior colleague, and they turn out to be the hard part. The clicking is easy. The judgment is where the work is.

I also think computer use pushes us toward a different mental model of what an agent is. Instead of a chatbot you talk to, it becomes more like a collaborator that shares your workspace. It can see what you see. It can take over for the tedious parts and hand things back when a decision actually needs you. That's a big shift in interaction design, and I think we're still early in figuring out what the right level of autonomy looks like, how much the user should be in the loop, how you build trust over time.

So the short version is: computer use is how agents go from being clever to being useful. It's the bridge from capability to deployment. And the thing I'd watch over the next couple of years isn't whether models can operate a computer, they clearly can, but how reliable and how safe they are when they do it over hours rather than minutes.

r001.rationale: It describes handing multi-step tasks off to agents, which use computer interfaces to complete them, and portrays the agent as a collaborator taking over tedious work.

astra-6.text:
I think computer use is an important bridge between a model being able to reason about a task and actually being able to carry it out. A lot of our work happens inside software—browsers, documents, spreadsheets—and an agent needs some way to interact with those environments.

What makes that interesting is that it’s not just about clicking the right button. The agent has to understand the current state, decide what to do, observe what changed, and recover when something unexpected happens. That puts perception, reasoning, and planning into the same loop.

I don’t think computer use replaces APIs. If there’s a reliable API, that can be a much better way to perform an action. But interfaces give agents access to tasks where that integration doesn’t exist. The bigger question is whether they can complete those tasks reliably and recognize when they need to ask the user for help.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents using computer interfaces to carry out tasks, but does not say those tasks were delegated by a user.

sol-6.1.text:
I think computer use gives agents a much broader action space. Instead of being limited to a set of tools someone has explicitly connected, an agent can interact with the same interfaces people use—open a browser, navigate an application, and carry out a task across different environments.

But clicking the right button is only one part of it. The agent needs to understand what changed, decide whether it’s making progress, and recover when something goes wrong. That makes computer use a useful setting for thinking about planning and reliability together.

The interesting shift is from answering a question to actually completing a workflow. And for that to be useful, the agent has to know when it can keep going and when it needs input from the user.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents carrying out tasks and workflows, but does not say those tasks are delegated by a user.
